reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as ill-defined erythematous patches with greasy yellowish scale in sebum-rich areas: scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears, and central chest
Mild scalp involvement manifests simply as dandruff, while more severe disease produces inflamed, scaly, sometimes itchy plaques
It has a characteristic bimodal age pattern, occurring in infants (including cradle cap) and again in adults
The condition is linked to the commensal yeast Malassezia, so antifungal agents are a mainstay of treatment

Management combines antifungal shampoos or creams with short courses of low-potency topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors for inflammation, and recognises that it is a relapsing condition needing maintenance
Unusually severe, extensive, or treatment-resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis should prompt consideration of underlying HIV infection or Parkinson's disease
Distinguish it from psoriasis (sharper, thicker, silvery plaques) and from atopic or contact dermatitis based on distribution and morphology
reference.pathophysiology: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder occurring in sebaceous-rich skin, driven by an abnormal host inflammatory response to Malassezia yeasts that are part of the normal skin flora. The yeasts metabolise sebum lipids, releasing free fatty acids and other products that irritate the skin and provoke inflammation in susceptible individuals. Sebaceous gland activity, an altered skin barrier, individual immune reactivity, and neurological or immunosuppressive comorbidities all influence expression. This explains its predilection for sebum-rich sites, its association with hormonal activity in infancy and adulthood, and its increased severity in HIV infection and Parkinson's disease.
additionalDifferentials: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus in atypical facial cases
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on distribution and greasy scale
Skin scrapings for mycology if dermatophyte infection is a consideration
HIV testing when disease is severe, sudden, or refractory
Skin biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain presentations
Assessment for neurological comorbidity such as Parkinson's disease when relevant
redFlags: Severe, extensive, or abrupt-onset disease prompting evaluation for immunosuppression such as HIV
Failure to respond to appropriate first-line therapy suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Secondary bacterial infection of excoriated or fissured plaques
reference.prognosis: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a benign but chronic relapsing condition; infantile disease usually resolves within months, whereas adult disease tends to persist with periodic flares and is controlled rather than cured.
pitfalls: Confusing it with psoriasis or dermatophyte infection and choosing the wrong therapy
Relying on topical corticosteroids alone and neglecting antifungal treatment of the yeast component
Overusing potent steroids on the face, risking atrophy and rosacea-like changes
Failing to investigate unusually severe or refractory disease for underlying HIV or neurological disease
management: Treat with topical antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or ciclopirox and medicated shampoos containing selenium sulphide, zinc pyrithione or coal tar as the mainstay
Add short courses of low-potency topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors to settle inflammation
Manage infantile cradle cap with emollients, gentle descaling and mild antifungal preparations
Use maintenance antifungal therapy to control this relapsing condition
Consider systemic antifungal therapy for severe or widespread disease
Investigate for underlying HIV infection or Parkinson's disease when disease is severe, sudden or treatment-resistant
